                          REPLY BRIEF OF U3 LANDOWNERS

       TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
       U3 Landowners file this Reply Brief and respectfully show as follows:


                                  I.      INTRODUCTION
       The initial briefs supporting Route 392, Route 410, or other alternatives share a common
analytical flaw. They declare that the threshold policy choice must be where the line crosses the
Colorado River, select Link U3, and then evaluate only the routes that survive that premise. But
the threshold question under PURA and the Commission’s rule is which complete route best
balances all applicable factors. One application of one routing criterion at one river crossing
cannot become dispositive merely because it is the feature on which Route 392 performs “best.”
The rest of the comparison is not close: Route 392 is 5.85 miles longer, costs $34.299 million
more, affects 51 more existing habitable structures, crosses more riparian area and more streams,
and encounters substantially more recorded cultural resources than Route 894.
       Route 894 remains the strongest record-supported choice. Applicants selected it after
evaluating the full filed route set under the statutory and regulatory criteria. Commission Staff
independently selected Route 487. Those recommendations differ only at the margins: Routes 894


PUC Docket No. 59475                                                   Reply Brief of U3 Landowners
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                    1
 and 487 share 32 links—roughly three-quarters of each route.1 Staff witness Poole may have
viewed U3’s transmission-line paralleling as a favorable feature, but Staff’s actual
recommendation is a complete route that crosses elsewhere.2 The intervenor briefs cannot convert
comments about one link into an institutional recommendation that Staff never made.
          A 765-kV line using Link U3 would not use the line, towers, or easement for the existing
transmission line. The old and existing line on U3 occupies an approximately 75-foot easement
and uses poles roughly 80 feet tall; the proposed 765-kV line requires an entirely new corridor
approximately 200 feet wide and structures up to 198 feet tall.3 BCI witness Sansom conceded
that paralleling the old line does not eliminate the new clearing, access, foundations, structures,
conductors, or disturbance.4 U3 may consolidate two corridors geographically, but it does not
avoid a new 200-foot disturbance across the Colorado River and adjoining land.
          Recent Commission precedent confirms the proper approach. In Docket No. 58276, the
Commission rejected a PFD that gave significant weight to a localized aesthetic concern and
selected the route that was cheaper, shorter, affected fewer habitable structures, and was superior
on the most objective environmental measurements.5 Here, the record presents an even stronger
and more comprehensive case against Route 392. The ALJs should select Routes 894 or 487.


    II.    THE COMMISSION MUST BALANCE COMPLETE ROUTES, NOT SINGLE
                                  FEATURES
          In Dunn v. Public Utility Commission of Texas, the Austin Court of Appeals rejected an
argument materially similar to the one advanced by Route 392 proponents in this proceeding.6 The
landowners in Dunn argued that the Commission’s failure to select one of two routes that paralleled
more existing rights-of-way and property lines than the selected route was arbitrary, capricious, an
abuse of discretion, and not supported by substantial evidence. The court rejected the premise that
a numerical advantage on a single criterion compels route selection regardless of the remaining

 evidence, holding that the rule does not permit “exclusive reliance on the numerical percentage”
of rights-of-way used or paralleled and that “no one factor controls or is dispositive.”7 The Route
392 proponents in this proceeding ask the ALJs to go further still: they elevate one application of
one routing criterion at a single stream crossing over the complete route comparison, even though
Route 392 costs $34.299 million more, affects 51 more habitable structures, and performs worse
on multiple environmental and cultural-resource measures.
        PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) require holistic route-selection
judgment. The Commission must consider community values, parks and recreational areas,
historical and aesthetic values, environmental integrity, engineering constraints, cost, prudent
avoidance, and the use of compatible corridors.          Dunn establishes that no single factor is
dispositive. The governing framework therefore does not permit Route 392’s proponents to
transform paralleling at U3 into a bright-line rule that automatically defeats every route crossing
the Colorado River elsewhere.
        The Commission’s rule expressly identifies three categories of compatible routing
opportunities: existing compatible rights-of-way, including existing transmission facilities; other
compatible rights-of-way, including roads, highways, and railroads; and property lines or other
natural or cultural features.8 The Applicants’ complete metric follows that framework and includes
existing electric lines, public roads and highways, railroads, and apparent property boundaries.9
The fact that Solana’s witness “declined”10 to use property-boundary data does not delete an
express rule criterion. Imperfect data may affect weight; it does not authorize a party to redefine
the legal standard around its preferred route.
        Docket No. 58276 is particularly instructive because the Commission confronted the same
structural error presented here: substantial weight placed on a localized qualitative impact at the
expense of the complete route comparison. The Commission did not disregard aesthetics when
deciding that case. Instead, it held that the factors had not been properly applied and selected the
route with the better overall combination of cost, habitable structures, length, and objective
environmental measurements.11 Route 894’s advantages over Route 392 are larger in absolute

miles of riparian area, and 14 recorded cultural-resource sites crossed.12
            Docket No. 55728 likewise demonstrates that party agreement and future-development
accommodations do not supersede the full routing balance. There, the parties supported or did not
oppose Route S, which was designed to accommodate intended future development and a
greenspace buffer. The Commission nevertheless selected Route H because it provided the better
overall balance, including fewer habitable structures and superior prudent-avoidance
performance.13 Plans for future development do not displace existing constraints merely because
the affected parties prefer another route.
            The older park cases14 cited by Route 392 proponents do not establish a contrary rule.
Docket No. 37448 ended with denial of the CCN application; its PFD discussion—now invoked
as precedent—was not a Commission selection of the route. Docket No. 38290 involved the
singular Palo Duro Canyon landscape and a route designed to bypass it. And Docket No. 45866
involved more than park aesthetics: the route selected by the Commission affected 24 fewer
habitable structures and paralleled a broad, developed corridor rather than a substantially narrower
county road. Those decisions confirm that qualitative impacts matter as part of the balance, not
that they erase the balance.


     III.    ROUTE 894 OUTPERFORMS ROUTES 392 AND 410 ON KEY ROUTE-WIDE

then hurry past the metrics on which it loses. The admitted differences are neither technical trivia
nor artifacts of one model. Route 894’s advantages span the criteria the Commission has
consistently treated as central—cost, prudent avoidance, length, compatible routing opportunities,
environmental integrity, parks, and cultural resources. Route 392’s proponents can prefer U3, but
they cannot make the rest of the filed comparison disappear. The table below summarizes the

           A.       Route 392’s prudent-avoidance disadvantage is substantial
           Route 392 affects 136 habitable structures within 500 feet, compared with 85 for Route
894. That is 51 additional existing structures—a 60 percent increase. Hodge-Schwertner witness
Andrews further explained that 124 of Route 392’s 136 structures are single-family residences and
that 40 single-family residences are concentrated along the 3.73-mile Link E12.16 Route 392
therefore does not accept additional cost to reduce residential exposure. Route 392 costs more
while placing the proposed line near more existing residences.


16
     Hodge-Schwertner Ex. 2 (Andrews Cross-Rebuttal) at 5–6.

PUC Docket No. 59475                                                              Reply Brief of U3 Landowners
SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349                             5
         BCI witness Turnbough called this difference “numerically insignificant” because the
routes exceed 200 miles,17 but neither the rule nor Commission precedent converts prudent
avoidance into a structures-per-mile statistic. Turnbough’s own prior testimony explains that
environmental criteria operationalize PURA and the Commission’s rule and that prudent
avoidance is measured by counting proximate habitable structures.18 Docket No. 58276 treated 23
structures as a material route difference. The 51-structure difference here is not made insignificant
by the length of the project. These are real homes with real people living inside. Staff’s own
routing analysis likewise treats fewer nearby habitable structures as affirmative prudent-avoidance
performance, explaining that limiting exposure may be accomplished by selecting a route with
fewer habitable structures near its centerline.19
        Solana witness Rhodes identified structure-data errors “on both sides”20 but did not
produce a corrected route-wide count showing that Route 392’s 51-structure disadvantage
disappears or materially narrows. He offered no basis to assume those errors affect Route 392
differently from other routes. Solana’s initial brief converts ordinary data uncertainty into a one-
way inference favoring Route 392 that the record does not support.


        B.       Estimated costs remain probative evidence
        The Route 392 proponents repeatedly reduce $34.299 million to “only two percent.”21
Ratepayers do not pay percentages; they pay dollars. Cost estimates in a CCN proceeding are
necessarily estimates, but that does not deprive them of evidentiary value. The Commission relied
on a $7.2 million estimated difference in Docket No. 58276.22                  Here, the Applicants used a
common estimating framework across the filed routes, and that framework shows Route 392 costs
$34.299 million more than Route 894. No party produced an estimate demonstrating the opposite.
        The cost critique is internally inconsistent. Rhodes first eliminated every non-U3 route,
narrowed the remaining U3 routes further, and then relied on cost and habitable structures to select

which route they favor.
         Route 410 is even less persuasive. The Applicants’ data show it is approximately $56.522

structures—13 more than Route 894. Its complete compatible-corridor percentage is also lower.25
Route 410’s lower habitable-structure count relative to Route 392 does not overcome its still-worse
performance on cost, length, prudent avoidance, and complete compatible-corridor use.


         C.       The route-wide environmental and cultural-resource data favor Route 894
         The Route 392 briefs focus myopically on the Colorado River crossing and park views.
Environmental integrity, however, applies to the complete route. Route 392 crosses 4.37 more
miles of riparian area, has 33 more stream crossings, crosses 14 more recorded cultural-resource
sites, and has 35 more recorded cultural resources within 1,000 feet than Route 894. Route 392—
not Route 894—also has measured mileage within the foreground visual zone of a park or
recreational area.26 Those standardized route-wide measures directly contradict the claim that
Route 392 is environmentally superior as a whole.
         BCI witness Turnbough’s own comparison underscores the problem. Of the eleven
differentiating metrics he listed for Routes 392 and 894, Route 392 was adverse on eight and Route
894 on three.27 Turnbough reached Route 392 only by giving decisive weight to U3’s supposed
advantages and minimizing most of the differences he identified. That is not a holistic application
of his own data. It is the single-feature approach the Commission rejected in Docket No. 58276.

         D.       Limited pipeline paralleling does not disqualify Routes 894 or 487
        Solana’s routing analysis treats pipeline paralleling as an exclusionary screen,28 but Staff
and Applicants do not. Staff witness Poole called it a “neutral factor”: paralleling existing
infrastructure may be beneficial, while AC-interference mitigation may also be required.29 He
confirmed that Staff’s Route 487 parallels approximately 2.04 miles of pipeline and Applicants’
Route 894 parallels approximately 2.29 miles.30 Pipeline paralleling therefore is neither prohibited
nor route-disqualifying; it is one engineering and cost consideration among many.
        Route 894’s approximately 2.29 miles of pipeline paralleling represents about one percent
of its 223.17-mile length.31 Solana witness Rhodes nevertheless eliminated five U3 routes because
of “extended” pipeline paralleling and then used the surviving subset to select Route 392.32 That
screen reflects his personal weighting of the criteria, not a statutory command. It cannot justify
eliminating Route 894 before a holistic comparison of the complete route set.


                   IV.      LINK U3 IS NOT AN IMPACT-FREE CORRIDOR
        A.       Route 894 crosses the river and leaves; Route 392 crosses it and remains in the
                 river system
        The pro-392 briefs repeatedly contrast a “new” crossing on J22 with an “existing corridor”
on U3.33 But Route 392 would not place the proposed 765-kV line on the existing structures or
within the existing line’s footprint. BCI witness Sansom acknowledged U3 would still involve a
new 200-foot project corridor and new clearing, access, foundations, structures, and conductors,
and he could not rule out the need for a new easement.34 Applicants confirmed that the proposed
765-kV line cannot be placed on the existing U3 structures; it will require new single-circuit steel
lattice towers and its own approximately 200-foot right-of-way, intended to abut—not overlap—
the existing corridor.35 Thus, every proposed river crossing—including U3—requires substantial

        The actual alignment between the river and the proposed line also matters. Commission
Staff witness Poole agreed that an environmental analysis should distinguish between a route that
simply crosses a river and one that continues along the river corridor for a substantial distance.36
He further agreed that a crossing that avoids following the river’s bends may be preferable to an
alignment that runs along the river corridor.37 Route 894 crosses the Colorado River on J22 at a
near-orthogonal angle and proceeds quickly away from the river in both directions. Route 392
crosses on U3, follows the river corridor for approximately two miles to the east, and continues
through streams, springs, ravines, and riparian features.38 The route-wide data confirm the point:
Route 392 has more riparian mileage and 33 more stream crossings.39 Route 894 crosses the
Colorado River and immediately leaves; Route 392 crosses it and remains intertwined with the
river system.


        B.      U3 crosses critical habitat and imposes site-specific impacts
        The Environmental Assessment’s Table 7-4 identifies Link U3 as crossing the Upper
Colorado River USFWS Critical Habitat Unit for the Texas pimpleback in San Saba and Lampasas
Counties.40 Route 392 uses U3; Route 894 does not. U3 also crosses the TPWD-designated
Ecologically Significant Stream Segment portion of the Colorado River, while Route 894’s J22
does not.41 Staff witness Poole agreed that if crossing the ESSS can be avoided, it should be.42
Thus, Route 392’s proponents claimed environmental advantage of U3 ignores another recognized
aquatic-resource constraint at that very crossing. The Applicants may be able to span waterways
and use best management practices, but mitigation is not avoidance. A brief cannot label U3 the
environmentally superior crossing while ignoring both federally designated critical habitat and a
TPWD-designated ESSS at the crossing it prefers.

          U3 also traverses rugged and operationally constrained land. On 3 Trees Ranch alone, the

ravines.      Record evidence describes repeated access, erosion, vegetation, and off-easement
disturbance associated with that smaller corridor.43                Those existing conditions do not become
irrelevant because the Route 392 proponents did not retain a witness to study them.

foot corridor over the representative 1,620-foot crossing would directly occupy approximately 7.44
acres of the quarry footprint and prevent ordinary extraction within that area, apart from additional
operational limitations outside the easement.44 This is not a request to adjudicate condemnation
damages. It is an existing productive land use that Applicant and Route 392 witnesses omitted
from their claimed landowner and environmental balance.


         C.       The complete compatible-corridor measure favors Route 894
         Route 392’s claimed paralleling advantage exists only after its proponents remove apparent
property boundaries from the Applicants’ complete compatible-corridor analysis. BCI Exhibit 61
sums transmission lines, roads, highways, and railroads, and treats that resulting subset as the only
“tangible” or meaningful corridor measure—but omits a category the Commission’s rule expressly
requires the ALJs to consider. On that self-selected subset,45 Route 392 performs better. On the
complete rule-recognized measure, it does not.
         At hearing, Mr. Poole agreed that apparent property boundaries can be imperfect. He also
confirmed that property-boundary paralleling is part of the Applicants’ data and that he considered
it in his analysis.46 Poole did not redefine compatible right-of-way or testify that existing
infrastructure alone controls route selection. Staff’s initial brief confirms the point: Staff evaluated
compatible rights-of-way and apparent property boundaries together, identified reduced landowner
impacts as a principal benefit of paralleling them, and relied on that combined measure in

which Route 894 performs materially better. The EA also explains why no corridor type can be
applied mechanically. Existing lines, roads, and property boundaries vary in width, use, terrain,
development, vegetation, and compatibility with a 765-kV facility. The Commission must
consider both quantity and quality. But qualitative judgment is a reason to examine the full
record—not a license to count only the corridors that favor one route and dismiss the rest as unreal.


         D.       The park record does not outweigh Route 894’s route-wide advantages
         Colorado Bend State Park and the planned Post Oak Ridge State Park are important
resources. The ALJs should consider credible visual and recreational evidence concerning them.
But Route 894 does not cross either park, and the standardized data show zero park or recreational
foreground-visual-zone mileage for Route 894 compared with 0.73 miles for Route 392.49 The
park evidence therefore does not establish the direct intrusion or objective route-wide superiority
necessary to override Route 894’s substantial advantages on cost, prudent avoidance, length,

                       VII.    PROPOSED CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. The Commission must consider and weigh the routing factors in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16
   TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). No single routing factor controls or is dispositive. Dunn v. Public
   Utility Commission of Texas, 246 S.W.3d 788,795-96 (Tex. App.-Austin 2008, no pet.).
2. Under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(i)-(iii), the Commission must consider existing compatible
   rights-of-way, other compatible rights-of-way, and property lines or other natural or cultural
   features when selecting a route.
3. The transmission facilities using Route 894 are necessary for the service, accommodation,
   convenience, or safety of the public within the meaning of PURA § 37.056(a) and 16 TAC §
   25.101.
4. Route 894 best meets the routing criteria in PURA § 37.056(c)(4) and 16 TAC §
   25.101(b)(3)(B), including the Commission's policy of prudent avoidance, to the extent
   reasonable to moderate the impact on the affected community and landowners.

                                         VIII.   CONCLUSION
        The aforementioned briefs identify impacts of Route 894, but they do not prove that
Route 392, Route 410, or another proposed alternative provides a better overall balance. Their
preferred result depends on a sequence of selective choices: make U3 mandatory, remove property
boundaries from the compatible-corridor metric, discount existing habitable structures, dismiss
cost when Route 392 is compared with Route 894-then restore cost as a meaningful criterion
when it helps select Route 392 from the preselected U3 routes-and examine the properties
avoided by Route 392 more closely than the properties that would receive the line. PURA and the
Commission's rule require the opposite approach: a comparison of the complete routes.
        The complete record shows that Route 894 is shorter and less expensive than Route 392,
affects 51 fewer habitable structures, parallels more compatible corridors, crosses less riparian area
and fewer streams, encounters fewer recorded cultural resources, avoids measured park-
foreground exposure, and avoids U3' s critical-habitat, ESSS, quarry, and access impacts. Route
410 fares no better: it is longer, more expensive, and affects 13 more habitable structures than
Route 894. Recent Commission precedent confirms that qualitative impacts and future plans are
part of the balance, not substitutes for it.
